name: Wendy Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Wendy, 43, and a junior electrician after leaving office supplies work. I have a vocational certificate, but I still need a senior to check my wiring and help me understand harder fault readings; I don't sign off installations. The firm pays above the usual rate, my partner Ben repairs bicycles, and with our children aged six and thirteen we've a mortgage and eight months of expenses saved. There are plenty of similar electrical jobs nearby; I sometimes use AI to explain a course term after a colleague showed me how, but checking the meaning with my booklet and senior takes longer than pressing the button.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a little office help is welcome if it leaves proper learning time on site. There's no need to sell us a new world because the appointment letter writes itself. I'd rather see a junior get a patient explanation than another faster target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our wages cover the mortgage and everyday bills, and eight months saved leaves a real margin. My shifts are regular and there are other employers nearby if I need to look. I feel secure enough to stay a learner instead of pretending I'm already good at everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my supervised wiring work through the next year. Now I'd ask to review the week's difficult drawings with my senior during Friday's normal shift, using the same checked booklet explanations I sometimes look up with AI. If that review wasn't agreed, I'd ask questions during the supervised task rather than add unpaid time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and pleased I can learn a practical job without fearing every mistake becomes a lost mortgage payment. It helps to have money behind the learning. I know some colleagues don't have that margin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What helps when you misunderstand a drawing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my senior to draw the bit I misunderstood and then let me explain it back. I'd rather admit I was confused on paper before touching the real installation. Being older than some of the crew doesn't make me better at the task.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you raise learning time with anyone else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the staff association that paid learning matters even when change is modest. I wouldn't claim the association had negotiated a new agreement just because I'd mentioned it. For now I'd keep doing the ordinary supervised work I am paid for.

say: I'd welcome modest **office help** if proper on-site learning time remains.
I'd value a **patient explanation** more than a new target based on a faster letter.
think: Our wages cover essentials, and **eight months saved** gives the household a real margin.
Regular shifts and **plentiful local employers** let me keep learning without pretending expertise I don't yet have.
do: Continue **supervised wiring work** through the next year.
Request a **Friday drawing review** inside normal paid hours, retaining task-level questions if refused.
feel: **Calm with financial room**, while aware that colleagues may lack the same margin for learning.
S0.quote: Being older than some of the crew doesn't make me better at the task.
fieldNote: Her **strong reserve** and high pay support secure learning without changing her junior standing or certificate-level education.
The paid review remains a **request**, and occasional AI explanations stay checked against established learning material and senior supervision.

steps.text: Continue supervised wiring with checked booklet explanations and drawing questions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say bookings and estimates can change before anyone replaces the hands on site. I'd ask the staff association to seek paid practice time when those changes are discussed. A new efficiency shouldn't mean the quickest learner gets help and everyone else gets a shorter shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my own hours and our household income to remain secure for now because both jobs are mostly hands-on. The office changes still make me uneasy about how junior workers get judged. I can afford to ask questions, but I'd like protection to come from agreed terms rather than my bank balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the association to collect junior workers' needs and propose a paid practice hour each month. In the first year I'd learn the firm's approved AI study aid only after my senior demonstrated it and confirmed how answers must be checked. I'd try it on six unfamiliar course terms, comparing each answer with the booklet before deciding whether it helped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the way the change might be managed, rather than frightened about my own next wage. I'm interested in a tool once I can see the checking method. I don't need to be the first person to press every button.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if an answer looked convincing but was wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the example and ask my senior to explain the error during the normal shift. I wouldn't keep using an answer just because I'd spent time finding it. If the errors made the tool more work than the booklet, I'd stop that trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should get the proposed practice time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the practice time to include people who need a slower explanation, not just the confident staff. The association would still need the employer to agree it. My savings aren't a substitute for somebody else's paid hour.

say: I'd distinguish **office changes** from the hands still needed on electrical sites.
I'd ask the **staff association** to include slower learners when seeking paid practice time.
think: Our **near-term wages** look secure because both household jobs remain mostly hands-on.
I'm uneasy about **junior assessments** and want agreed protection rather than reliance on personal savings.
do: Seek a **paid practice hour** monthly through the association after gathering junior workers' needs.
Learn the **approved study aid** after demonstration, checking six terms against the booklet before wider use.
feel: **Uneasy but interested**, willing to try a demonstrated tool while secure about the next wage.
S1.quote: My savings aren't a substitute for somebody else's paid hour.
fieldNote: She separates **personal income security** from a collective concern about learning conditions and staff assessment.
The **six-term trial** preserves demonstration and source checking; it never gives AI authority to approve electrical work.

steps.text: Seek a monthly paid practice hour through the staff association
Learn the approved study aid after demonstration and six checked terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the association the office side faces the 2028 change before capable robots reach physical work around 2031. We should negotiate before each group is already losing hours. I'd include learners like me without forgetting the people who keep the bookings straight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own paid hours could shrink when robots can do the fitting, and Ben's bicycle work could change too. Eight months of costs saved gives us room to respond, not a promise that both wages remain intact. I don't expect to be helpless, but I'd stop treating the current wage as the whole family plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd enrol in a short supervised drawing-reading course, paying from our separate study allowance while keeping the eight-month reserve intact. During 2029 I'd apply for actual paid supervised maintenance vacancies only if the written hours and pay covered our basic bills. I'd also help the association seek notice and paid transition training, without counting those proposed terms as agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with some real room to choose. I can pay for the small course and still cover the house if it doesn't lead anywhere. That doesn't make the later wage question disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make that short course useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask which parts I could actually practise and have checked, not whether the certificate sounded impressive. A short course wouldn't make me a licensed independent electrician. I'd still need supervised work and a real vacancy, and I'd compare that work with what robots might change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide whether the household could afford a bigger change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ben and I would check both actual wages and the mortgage before committing to anything bigger. I wouldn't promise that bicycle repairs would replace my income, or that my electrical hours would replace Ben's. Two physical jobs aren't an insurance policy written by a machine forecast.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 office tasks** from capable robots reaching physical work around 2031.
I'd seek **notice and paid training** before workers' hours are already lost.
think: Either household job could lose **physical hours later**, so current wages cannot be the whole plan.
Our **eight-month reserve** offers choices without guaranteeing both incomes remain intact.
do: Enrol in the **supervised drawing course** now from a separate allowance, preserving emergency savings.
Apply for **2029 supervised vacancies** only on written hours and pay covering basic bills.
Seek notice and **paid transition training** through the association without assuming approval.
feel: **Anxious with choices**, able to fund a small experiment while recognising it doesn't answer the later wage question.
S2.quote: A short course wouldn't make me a licensed independent electrician.
fieldNote: She preserves **junior qualification limits** and treats paid work after study as conditional on real vacancies and supervision.
The **course budget** is separate from the protected reserve, while both household wages remain possible sources of later risk.

steps.text: Take the supervised drawing course from the separate study allowance
Seek paid supervised maintenance vacancies in 2029 on bill-covering written terms
Seek notice and paid transition training through the staff association

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us find out whether training actually helps before calling it a solution. We'd still need agreed notice and paid learning. The thinking systems arrive in 2031 and capable robots around 2034, so the site team's extra time shouldn't delay support for the office team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our own pay and savings look secure over the next few years, and I can test a small course while keeping my wage. I'm uneasy about making a wrong choice for the later years, not expecting an immediate household income loss. There's time to look at actual jobs without jumping at the first encouraging brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the supervised drawing course now from the separate allowance, keeping all my basic shifts. I'd ask the association to continue seeking paid transition terms for site and office staff. In 2032 I'd apply for real supervised maintenance vacancies only if written hours and pay covered the household basics, reviewing the value of any further course before paying for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not in a hurry to spend money to feel prepared. I can finish one course and ask whether I understand more than before. A longer runway gives me time to say no to the next course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge whether the course helped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare my own marked drawings from the first and last weeks and ask the tutor where I still needed help. Passing a class wouldn't prove an employer needed another junior. I'd look for actual paid hours as well as evidence that I had improved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why seek shared funding if your household can pay for this course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say our ability to pay for a small course doesn't mean everyone should be sent away to buy one. Shared paid training would make preparation less dependent on family savings. I'd help gather what colleagues needed before the association put the proposal forward.

say: I'd use **five years** to test training rather than call the first course a complete solution.
I'd avoid making **office staff** wait for the site team's later physical deadline.
think: Our **near-term pay** and reserve look secure while I test a small course alongside wages.
I'm uneasy about a **wrong later choice**, with time to check real jobs before buying more study.
do: Take the **supervised drawing course** from the separate allowance, keeping every basic shift.
Continue seeking **paid transition terms** through the association for both site and office staff.
Seek **2032 vacancies** only with paid supervision and written hours and pay covering household basics.
feel: **Uneasy but unhurried**, able to judge one course before deciding whether another deserves money.
S3.quote: A longer runway gives me time to say no to the next course.
fieldNote: Lower distress follows explicit **near-term security** and room for a limited experiment, not an assumed successful career transition.
She separates **family affordability** from fair shared terms and still requires real paid supervision before changing work.

steps.text: Take supervised drawing study from the separate allowance while retaining all basic paid shifts
Seek paid transition terms for site and office staff through the association
Seek supervised maintenance vacancies in 2032 on household-covering written terms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends ten years should make learning feel ordinary instead of a personal emergency. I'd still ask for paid time through the association. Having a longer warning isn't a reason to leave the slower learners paying for everything alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work and household money feel secure over the next few years, and the chance to become steadier at this trade looks good for me. I'll be 53 when thinking AGI arrives in 2036, still needing earnings when robots follow around 2039. I can prepare without pretending I know which job I'll hold then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the short drawing course now and keep ordinary supervised shifts. Each year we'd review both wages, the reserve and actual vacancies before paying for more study, while the association kept seeking paid learning. During 2037 I'd apply for a suitable supervised maintenance vacancy only on written terms covering our basic bills; I'd stay with better current work if there wasn't one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own position and interested in becoming better at something I chose. I still care what happens to people with less room. I can enjoy our children's school years without turning every birthday into a deadline for machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change the plan before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare actual paid hours and what the firms had really ordered, rather than use a video as a staffing plan. If our hours weakened sooner, we'd bring the advice or vacancy checks forward. The annual review is a reminder to look, not a ban on acting between dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the children I still needed somebody to check my work and wasn't ashamed of that. I wouldn't promise that any subject guaranteed a safe lifetime job. I'd help with the next real school choice rather than ask them to solve 2039 now.

say: I'd seek **ordinary paid learning** rather than treat a decade of preparation as an individual emergency.
I'd ask the association to include **slower learners**, even when the warning is long.
think: My own **near-term position** feels secure, and time to improve at the trade looks positive.
At **53 in 2036**, I'll still need future earnings without knowing which job will provide them.
do: Take the **drawing course** now while keeping ordinary supervised shifts.
Review actual wages and vacancies annually while pursuing **paid learning** through the association.
Seek a suitable **2037 supervised vacancy** only on written terms covering basic bills, retaining better current work if appropriate.
feel: **Calm and interested** in her own progress, while still concerned about colleagues with less financial room.
S4.quote: I can enjoy our children's school years without turning every birthday into a deadline for machines.
fieldNote: Calm reflects **personal security** and affordable improvement, rather than a claim that later automation cannot affect her work.
Her **2037 option** stays conditional, and annual household checks can bring action forward when actual income changes sooner.

steps.text: Take supervised drawing study from the separate allowance while keeping ordinary electrical shifts
Seek paid learning through the staff association during preparation years
Seek suitable supervised vacancies in 2037 on bill-covering written terms

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because our physical work could change around 2031 before I've tested many alternatives. Agreed notice, paid learning and actual supervised vacancies would help, with the family reserve kept for the house rather than endless speculative courses. My children need a home while I practise, not a certificate pile instead of a mortgage payment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a learner can be well paid and still need a basic explanation. I can, and pretending otherwise would be dangerous. I'd rather have honest checking than perform confidence for a customer.

headlineQuote: My children need a home while I practise, not a certificate pile instead of a mortgage payment.
portrait: At **43**, Wendy is a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, higher pay, and eight months of household expenses saved.
She and **Ben**, her bicycle-mechanic partner, have two school-age children and a mortgage, with plenty of nearby electrical employers.
She uses **AI occasionally** for checked explanations and prefers demonstrated tools, supervised practice and limited affordable study.
Her **progressive outlook** supports shared paid learning; strong personal finances permit calmer preparation without assuming lifelong security or automatic promotion.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time to test alternatives before capable robots could affect both physical household jobs around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Agreed notice**, paid learning and real supervised vacancies would help while protecting the household reserve from speculative course spending.
